(By Smt.Padma S Uttur, Adv.,)
 JUDGMENT
This petition under Section 166 MV act is filed by the Petitioner seeking compensation of Rs.25,00,000/- for the injuries sustained in a road traffic accident.

2.It is the specific case of the petitioner that on 25-05-2023 at about 2.30 p.m., while he was walking on the extreme side of the road from Baguru towards his village on Baguru-Channarayapatna road,
near Kuruvanka, the rider of motorcycle bearing registration No. KA-13-EW-5501 (hereinafter referred to as the offending two wheeler) came at a high speed, rode the same in a rash and negligent manner, and dashed the petitioner from behind.
3. Due to the impact, the petitioner fell on the road and sustained grievous injuries.

Immediately after the accident, he was shifted to Grasslife Health care Hospital, at Channarayapatana, and thereafter admitted to KIMS hospital, Bengaluru, where he was treated as an inpatient and underwent surgery.
4. It is stated that due to the accidental injuries, the petitioner has suffered permanent disability and is unable to lead his normal life as he did prior to the accident.

The petitioner has further contended that he incurred an expenditure of about Rs. 80,000/- towards medical treatment, medicines,
conveyance, and other incidental expenses.
5. At the time of the accident, the petitioner was aged about 36 years, working as a driver and agriculturist, earning a monthly income of Rs.42,000/-.
Due to the permanent disability, he has suffered loss of earning capacity and loss of income.

6. As the accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent riding of the rider of the offending vehicle,xz the petitioner has sought compensation from Respondent No. 1, the owner/insured of the offending vehicle, and Respondent No. 2, the insurer of the said vehicle.
7. In response to the petition notice, the Respondent No.2 had appeared before the court through its counsel and filed the objections.
The respondent No.1 has not appeared and he was placed exparte.

8. Respondent No. 2, the insurer, in its written statement, has denied the issuance of an insurance policy in respect of the offending vehicle and stated that, if any policy exists, its liability is strictly subject to the terms and conditions thereof.
It has denied the involvement of offending motorcycle in the accident.

sentences.text: It is further contended that the accident occurred due to the negligence of the petitioner himself.

Respondent No. 2 has also alleged that the rider of the offending vehicle was not holding a valid and effective driving licence as on the date of the accident, thereby violating the policy conditions.
The respondent has also denied the nature of injuries, avocation, income, disability, and medical expenses claimed by the petitioner.
Hence, Respondent No. 2 has prayed for dismissal of the claim petition.

10. On the basis of the above pleadings, the following Issues were framed :-
1.

Whether the Petitioner proves that on 25-05-2023 at about 02-30 p.m., at Baguru channarayapatna Road, near Kuruvanka, he sustained injuries in a road traffic accident, while he was walking by the side of the road, due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the motorcycle bearing No.KA 13-EW-5501?
2. Whether the respondent No.2 proves that there is violation of the policy conditions by respondent No.1 and respondent No.2 is not liable to pay any compensation?
3. Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
if any, how much, from whom?
4. What order or award ?
11. In order to prove the claim, the Petitioner examined himself as PW.1 and in support of his case, 4 witnesses were examined as PW-2 to 5 and got marked the documents as per Ex.P.1 to P.27.
On the other hand, the Respondent No.2 has examined the MRO at Grosslife hospital as RW-1 and got marked the documents at Ex.R1 t o 4.
Further, the CMO at KIMS hospital is examined as RW-2 and one document is marked as Ex.R.5.

Respondent No.2 has examined its official as RW-3 and got marked the documents at Ex.R.6 and 7.
12.

By considering the available materials on record and the arguments addressed by the parties, I have answered the above Issues as under:
13.

My findings to the above issues are as under:
Issue No.1: In the Affirmative.
Issue No.2: In the Negative.
Issue No.3: Partly in the affirmative.
Issue No.4: As per the final order, for the following:

REASONS 14. ISSUE NO.1:- It is the specific case of the petitioner that on 25-05-2023 at about 2.30 p.m.,
while he was walking on the extreme side of the road from Baguru towards his village on Baguru- Channarayapatna road, near Kuruvanka, the rider of the offending two wheeler came at a high Sanvith Gowda.

3 speed, rode the same in a rash and negligent manner, and dashed the petitioner from behind.
Due to the impact, the petitioner fell on the road and sustained grievous injuries.
15. To substantiate his case, the petitioner examined himself as PW-1 and filed an affidavit in lieu of examination-in-chief under Order XVIII Rule 4 of CPC, reiterating the contents of the petition.

He produced the FIR at Ex.P1, FIS at Ex.P2, Spot and seizure Mahazar at Ex.P3, IMV report at Ex.P4,
Wound Certificate at Ex.P5, Notice and Reply Notice at Ex.P6 and P7 and Charge Sheet at Ex.P8.
16.
Dr. D.S. Ramachandra was examined as PW-5, who produced two documents marked as Exhibits P-26 and P-27.
The Administrator of Grass Life Hospital was examined as PW-3 and produced medical records marked as Exhibits P-22 to P-25.
The Medical Record Technician of KIMS Hospital was examined as PW-4, who produced the case sheet, copy of the MLC register extract, and X-ray of the petitioner.
As per the wound certificate at Exhibit P-5, the petitioner sustained multiple grievous injuries.
17. To further support his case, the petitioner examined an eyewitness as PW-2, who deposed that the rider of the offending two-wheeler came at a high speed and dashed against the petitioner.

According to PW-2, due to the impact, the petitioner sustained severe injuries to his chest, head,
abdomen, and left hand, and the accident occurred due to the rash and negligent riding of the rider of the offending two- wheeler.

18. The core defence of Respondent No. 2 is that the offending motorcycle was not involved in the accident and that the petitioner sustained injuries due to a skid and fall, followed by a false implication of the vehicle to claim compensation.
In support of this contention, the official of the Respondent no 2 was examined as RW 3.
he has reiterated above said contention.
19. The contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that a mere reference in Exhibit P-11 and Ex.P.19 cannot, by itself, defeat the claim deserves acceptance.
It is well settled that the history recorded in medical documents is primarily meant for clinical management and is generally based on information furnished by the patient or attendants.
Such an entry cannot outweigh the probative value of police records prepared after investigation, particularly when the latter consistently support the petitioner's case.
In this regard, reliance placed on the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka reported in 2018 (1) KCCR 351 - Yellappa @ Shivappa Sajali v. Ashoka Bhalappa Nayak and another.

sentences.text: The oral evidence of PW1 and PW2 remains consistent and mutually corroborative.
Their testimony aligns with the police records, and no material contradiction has been brought out in cross- examination.
The contention that PW2 is not an eyewitness is disproved by the charge sheet itself, wherein PW2 is cited as a witness no 3.
The defence theory of skid and fall and subsequent false projection as a pedestrian remains unsupported by any independent evidence.
21. The medical evidence establishes that the petitioner sustained multiple grievous injuries indicative of a forceful impact.
No contrary medical opinion has been produced to discredit this evidence.

Although Exhibits P-19 and P-11 contain a reference to skid and fall, the admission elicited from RW2 clearly establishes that the history recorded therein was based solely on information furnished by the petitioner's wife and not on any independent assessment.
Such entries, being intended for clinical management, cannot override investigative records prepared after due inquiry.
22. RW-1, the Medical Records Officer of Grass Life Hospital, RW 2 the CMO of KIMS hospital were examined by the respondent no 2 and the MLC register was produced.
RW1 and RW2 were treated as hostile, and during cross-examination it was suggested to RW1 that certain pages in the MLC(EX R4) were not filled and that some pages were left blank.
Mere non-filling of certain pages or blank pages in the MLC register (EX R4) does not render the document unreliable nor does it demolish the petitioner's case.
If the respondent no 2 had serious doubts regarding manipulation or misrepresentation, they could have initiated appropriate proceedings, which admittedly has not been done.
It was suggested to RW2 during cross- examination that the history of the accident recorded in Exhibit P-19 was based on the information furnished by the petitioner's wife.
RW2 has admitted the said suggestion, and the relevant portion of the recitals were accordingly marked as Exhibit P-19(a to c).

This admission clearly establishes that the history noted in Exhibit P-19 was not based on any independent verification or investigation by the hospital authorities, but solely on the information supplied by the attendant.
As already observed, the primary purpose of recording such history in medical records is for clinical management and not for determination of fault or manner of the accident.

Therefore, the entry relating to "skid and fall" in Exhibit P-11 and P.19, having been admittedly based on third-party information, cannot be treated as conclusive or decisive to discredit the consistent police records and the oral evidence adduced by the petitioner.

On the contrary, this admission further weakens the defence of the respondent No.2 that the accident occurred due to skid and fall and strengthens the case of the petitioner regarding the involvement of the offending vehicle.

23. The documentary evidence prepared in the normal course of official duty namely the FIR,
complaint, spot mahazar, IMV report, wound certificate, notice, reply notice, and charge sheet uniformly attributes the cause of the accident to rash and negligent riding of the offending motorcycle.
These documents carry a statutory presumption of correctness and have not been challenged before any competent forum.
24. The allegation of collusion between the petitioner, his brother-in-law is a serious charge, but it remains wholly unsubstantiated.

No complaint, inquiry, or independent material has been produced Sanvith Gowda.M vs Karthik Gowda M.B on 5 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/42589307/
5 to support this allegation.

sentences.text: Mere assertions without proof cannot be accepted.
25. As regards the delay in lodging the complaint, the delay is one day and stands satisfactorily explained by the petitioner's medical condition.
Such a short delay does not assume significance when the overall evidence is consistent and reliable.
26. The respondent has placed reliance on the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 32138 of 2018, New India Assurance Company Ltd. v. Velu and Others.

entities.text: New India Assurance Company Ltd. v. Velu and Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court, on appreciation of the evidence, found that all the available material, including discharge summaries and police records, consistently pointed towards a skid and fall, and that the FIR itself was lodged after an inordinate delay of 30 days.

In those circumstances,
the Tribunal had dismissed the claim petition and the same was affirmed.
27. It is evident that the factual foundation of the present case materially differs from the decision relied upon by Respondent No. 2.
In the cited case, all contemporaneous records uniformly pointed towards a skid and fall, coupled with an unexplained delay of 30 days in lodging the FIR.

In the present case, except for isolated references in Ex.P.11 and P.19 (KIMS hospital medical documents),
the contemporaneous evidence consistently points towards a road traffic accident involving the offending motorcycle and the petitioner was a pedestrian .
28. In motor accident claim proceedings, the standard of proof is one of preponderance of probabilities.

When the evidence on record is assessed on this standard, the petitioner's case is fully supported by oral testimony, wound certificate - Ex.R.2 and 3, and police documents, whereas the defence raised by Respondent No. 2 lacks evidentiary support.
29. For the foregoing reasons, this Tribunal holds that the petitioner has successfully proved that the accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent riding of the offending motorcycle.
The defence that the accident occurred due to a skid and fall or that the offending vehicle was falsely implicated is not proved.
Accordingly, Issue No. 1 is answered in the affirmative.

30. ISSUE NO.2:- Respondent No. 2 contended that the owner of the offending motorcycle violated the terms and conditions of the insurance policy, and therefore, the insurance company cannot be held liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.

Respondent No. 2 has not established any statutory defence available under Section 149(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, such as absence of a valid driving licence or fundamental breach of policy conditions, by leading acceptable evidence.
In the absence of proof of such breach, the insurer cannot avoid its statutory obligation to indemnify the insured.
31. Further this Tribunal holds that Respondent No. 2 has failed to prove that it is entitled to be absolved from liability.
The insurance policy covering the offending vehicle was valid as on the date of the accident, and no breach of policy conditions has been established.
Consequently, Respondent No. 2, being the insurer of the offending vehicle, is liable to indemnify the insured and satisfy the award passed in favour of the petitioner.
Accordingly, Respondent No. 2 is liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.
Hence I answer issue no.2 in the Negative.

sentences.text: Thereafter, he was referred and admitted to KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru, where he underwent further treatment and surgical intervention.

33. PW5, Dr. Ramachandra, Orthopaedic Surgeon and DNB (PG) Teacher at General Hospital,
Jayanagar, Bengaluru, deposed that the petitioner sustained injuries in a road traffic accident and was treated as an inpatient at KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru.

He has categorically stated that the petitioner suffered fracture of the shaft left humerus with medial epicondyle fracture (Type II)
compound Monteggia fracture dislocation of the left forearm, fracture of the right clavicle, fracture of the right 6th rib, and bilateral subpleural consolidation with right-sided subpleural pneumonitis.
34.

On examination, the petitioner complained of difficulty in lifting objects , eating in the Indian style, combing and plaiting hair, wearing shirts, performing ablution, holding a glass of water, and writing.

PW5 assessed the permanent disability of the right and left upper limbs together at 63.6%
and assessed the whole- body disability at 21.2%.
35. During the course of cross-examination, PW5 admitted that he had not personally treated the petitioner and had not examined the inpatient or outpatient records in detail.
He further admitted that the petitioner had taken treatment at KIMS Hospital and had undergone surgical procedures therein.

He also admitted that no surgery was conducted for the clavicle fracture or rib fractures and denied the suggestion that malunion of the clavicle and ribs was caused due to non-suggestion of Sanvith Gowda.M vs Karthik Gowda M.B on 5 January, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/42589307/

sentences.text: He further admitted that the range of movements varies from person to person and denied the suggestion that a restriction of movement of 9% is negligible.
He also admitted that scar marks by themselves do not constitute disability, but clarified that the assessed disability includes the cumulative effect of all fractures sustained by the petitioner.
36. On an overall appreciation of the medical evidence, it is evident that the injuries sustained by the petitioner to both upper limbs have resulted in restricted mobility and locomotor impairment.
The upper limbs are vital for performing day-to-day activities as well as occupational tasks, and any impairment to these limbs inevitably affects functional efficiency.
However, PW5 has not expressed any specific opinion regarding the functional disability, namely, the actual impact of the injuries on the petitioner's earning capacity.
37. It is also relevant that the petitioner was a driver and agriculturist.
His work involves movement and physical activity to some extent, and the residual pain and restriction would reasonably affect his efficiency.
However, considering that the petitioner has recovered to a fair extent and can manage normal activities, it would not be appropriate to adopt the full limb disability as functional disability.

Taking into consideration the nature and location of the injuries, the degree of disability sustained, its functional impact on daily and vocational activities, the age and avocation of the petitioner, this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that the functional disability should be reasonably assessed at 11% to the whole body, rather than 21.2% as assessed purely on physical grounds.
This assessment shall be taken into account for the purpose of computing compensation for future loss of earning capacity.
38. In the petition the age of the petitioner is mentioned as 36 years.

Ex.P.14 - Aadhar card of the petitioner shows that he was born on 06-07-1987, the same is considered, then age of the petitioner as on the date of accident as 36 years and the multiplier applicable to the case on hand is 15.
39.
It is the specific case of the petitioner that at the time of the accident, he was aged about 36 years and working as a driver as well as agricultural activities and was earning 42,000/-p.m.
In order to substantiate his employment and income, the petitioner has not produced any supportive documents.
40. In the absence of concrete evidence relating to the petitioner's income, the Tribunal is required to adopt the notional income as per the guidelines of Lokadalath.
Considering that the accident occurred in the year 2023, the petitioner's notional monthly income is assessed at Rs.16,000/- for the purpose of calculating compensation.

41. Thus this tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner who sustained the injuries is entitled for compensation under the following heads:
42. Loss of future income on account of permanent disability: Considering the petitioner's grievous injury which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, this court is of the opinion that the functional disability of 11% is reasonable and just.

The petitioner was 36 years old as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 15.
The notional income taken as Rs.16,000 x 12 x 15 x 11/100= Rs.3,16,800/- towards loss of future income.
44. Pain and sufferings:

So far as the compensation under non-pecuniary damages are concerned,
considering the nature of the injuries, which has resulted in difficulty in mobility and in performing daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of inpatient treatment and physical and mental suffering endured by the petitioner, this tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of .40,000/-
would be just and fair compensation under the head pain and sufferings.
45. Loss of amenities of life: undoubtedly the petitioner is suffering from difficulties in performing day to day activities and is facing continuous hardship due to the disability.
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .30,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
46. Medical expenses:
Under the pecuniary damages, expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization and medicines, the Petitioner has relied on medical bills at Ex.P.15 for Rs.1,61,873/-.
On perusal of these medical bills, it reveals that the Petitioner has spent .1,61,873/- towards medical expenses.
The medical bills appears to be genuine.
Therefore, the Petitioner is entitled for medical expenses of .1,61,873/- towards Medical Expenses.
47. Future medical expenses:
PW5 has stated that the petitioner requires 3 more surgeries for removal of implant from Shaft of left humerus, medial epicondyle of lower end of left humerus and olecranon process of left ulna.
Considering the potential future surgery, this tribunal is of the opinion that it would be just and reasonable to award Rs. 30,000/- towards future medical expenses.
48. Conveyance, food and nourishment charges:
Ex.P.11 -Discharge summary shows that Petitioner underwent inpatient treatment at KIMS hospital, Bengaluru from 26-05-2023 to 14-06-2023 i.e, for a period of 20 days.
Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award compensation of .20,000/- under the head of conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges.
49. Loss of earning during laid up period:

With regard to the loss of earnings during treatment period, Considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in significant difficulty in carrying out daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of impatient treatment and recovery,
this tribunal considers the 3 months for rest is considered .

As the monthly income of the Petitioner is already considered as .16,000/- per month, loss of earning during laid up period would be .16,000 x 3 = Rs.48,000/-.
50.

Liability:
Respondent No.1 being the insured and the Respondent No.2 being the insurer of the offending vehicle are jointly and severally liable to pay the above compensation.

However,
Respondent No.2 is liable to pay compensation to the Petitioner with interest at 6% p.a.

52. ISSUE NO.4 :

In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to above issues,
I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
Claim Petition filed under Sec.166 of M.V.Act is allowed in part with cost.

Petitioner is awarded compensation of Rs.6,46,673/- together with interest @ 6% p.a.
(except future medical expenses) from the date of petition till the date of deposit with the Tribunal.
Respondent No.2 shall pay the aforesaid amount within two months from the date of this order.
After deposit of the compensation amount, 25% of the amount shall be kept in FD in the name of petitioner in any nationalized or scheduled bank of his choice for a period of 2 years.
Remaining 75% amount shall be disbursed to the petitioner through E- payment on proper identification.
Advocate's fee is fixed at .1,000/-.
Draw award accordingly.

opennyai_summary.issue:
Whether the Petitioner proves that on 25-05-2023 at about 02-30 p.m., at Baguru channarayapatna Road, near Kuruvanka, he sustained injuries in a road traffic accident, while he was walking by the side of the road, due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the motorcycle bearing No.KA 13-EW-5501?
2. Whether the respondent No.2 proves that there is violation of the policy conditions by respondent No.1 and respondent No.2 is not liable to pay any compensation?
3. Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
if any, how much, from whom?
4. What order or award ?
REASONS 14. ISSUE NO.1:- It is the specific case of the petitioner that on 25-05-2023 at about 2.30 p.m.,

opennyai_summary.arguments:
It is well settled that the history recorded in medical documents is primarily meant for clinical management and is generally based on information furnished by the patient or attendants.
Such an entry cannot outweigh the probative value of police records prepared after investigation, particularly when the latter consistently support the petitioner's case.
In this regard, reliance placed on the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka reported in 2018 (1) KCCR 351 - Yellappa @ Shivappa Sajali v. Ashoka Bhalappa Nayak and another.
26. The respondent has placed reliance on the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 32138 of 2018, New India Assurance Company Ltd. v. Velu and Others.
The petitioner was 36 years old as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 15.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
2) 2020 ACJ 1916 (KAL) - National Ins.Co.Ltd., Vs. Shila Debi and others.
3) 2021 ACJ 1309 (HYD) - Vojje Mahankali Vs. M.Satyanarayana and another.
As already observed, the primary purpose of recording such history in medical records is for clinical management and not for determination of fault or manner of the accident.
Therefore, the entry relating to "skid and fall" in Exhibit P-11 and P.19, having been admittedly based on third-party information, cannot be treated as conclusive or decisive to discredit the consistent police records and the oral evidence adduced by the petitioner.
These documents carry a statutory presumption of correctness and have not been challenged before any competent forum.
Mere assertions without proof cannot be accepted.
25. As regards the delay in lodging the complaint, the delay is one day and stands satisfactorily explained by the petitioner's medical condition.
Such a short delay does not assume significance when the overall evidence is consistent and reliable.
In the cited case, all contemporaneous records uniformly pointed towards a skid and fall, coupled with an unexplained delay of 30 days in lodging the FIR.
28. In motor accident claim proceedings, the standard of proof is one of preponderance of probabilities.
When the evidence on record is assessed on this standard, the petitioner's case is fully supported by oral testimony, wound certificate - Ex.R.2 and 3, and police documents, whereas the defence raised by Respondent No. 2 lacks evidentiary support.
30. ISSUE NO.2:- Respondent No. 2 contended that the owner of the offending motorcycle violated the terms and conditions of the insurance policy, and therefore, the insurance company cannot be held liable to pay compensation to the petitioner.
Respondent No. 2 has not established any statutory defence available under Section 149(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, such as absence of a valid driving licence or fundamental breach of policy conditions, by leading acceptable evidence.
In the absence of proof of such breach, the insurer cannot avoid its statutory obligation to indemnify the insured.
The insurance policy covering the offending vehicle was valid as on the date of the accident, and no breach of policy conditions has been established.
The upper limbs are vital for performing day-to-day activities as well as occupational tasks, and any impairment to these limbs inevitably affects functional efficiency.
However, PW5 has not expressed any specific opinion regarding the functional disability, namely, the actual impact of the injuries on the petitioner's earning capacity.
37. It is also relevant that the petitioner was a driver and agriculturist.
His work involves movement and physical activity to some extent, and the residual pain and restriction would reasonably affect his efficiency.
However, considering that the petitioner has recovered to a fair extent and can manage normal activities, it would not be appropriate to adopt the full limb disability as functional disability.
Taking into consideration the nature and location of the injuries, the degree of disability sustained, its functional impact on daily and vocational activities, the age and avocation of the petitioner, this Tribunal is of the considered opinion that the functional disability should be reasonably assessed at 11% to the whole body, rather than 21.2% as assessed purely on physical grounds.
In order to substantiate his employment and income, the petitioner has not produced any supportive documents.
40. In the absence of concrete evidence relating to the petitioner's income, the Tribunal is required to adopt the notional income as per the guidelines of Lokadalath.
Considering that the accident occurred in the year 2023, the petitioner's notional monthly income is assessed at Rs.16,000/- for the purpose of calculating compensation.
41. Thus this tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner who sustained the injuries is entitled for compensation under the following heads:
42. Loss of future income on account of permanent disability: Considering the petitioner's grievous injury which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, this court is of the opinion that the functional disability of 11% is reasonable and just.
Sanvith Gowda.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .30,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
Considering the potential future surgery, this tribunal is of the opinion that it would be just and reasonable to award Rs. 30,000/- towards future medical expenses.
Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award compensation of .20,000/- under the head of conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges.
With regard to the loss of earnings during treatment period, Considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in significant difficulty in carrying out daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of impatient treatment and recovery,
this tribunal considers the 3 months for rest is considered .
As the monthly income of the Petitioner is already considered as .16,000/- per month, loss of earning during laid up period would be .16,000 x 3 = Rs.48,000/-.
50.
Thus the compensation awarded under the various heads are as under:

Liability:
Respondent No.1 being the insured and the Respondent No.2 being the insurer of the offending vehicle are jointly and severally liable to pay the above compensation.
However,
Respondent No.2 is liable to pay compensation to the Petitioner with interest at 6% p.a.
52. ISSUE NO.4 :
In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to above issues,
I proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
Claim Petition filed under Sec.166 of M.V.Act is allowed in part with cost.
Petitioner is awarded compensation of Rs.6,46,673/- together with interest @ 6% p.a.
(except future medical expenses) from the date of petition till the date of deposit with the Tribunal.
Respondent No.2 shall pay the aforesaid amount within two months from the date of this order.
After deposit of the compensation amount, 25% of the amount shall be kept in FD in the name of petitioner in any nationalized or scheduled bank of his choice for a period of 2 years.
Remaining 75% amount shall be disbursed to the petitioner through E- payment on proper identification.
Advocate's fee is fixed at .1,000/-.
Draw award accordingly.
